raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"No. A molecule binding at an allosteric site does not necessarily inhibit an enzyme, because allosteric regulators can either inhibit or activate it. Allosteric sites are locations on an enzyme away from the active site, and binding there induces a conformational change [ev_001]. An allosteric inhibitor binds away from the active site and induces a conformational change that reduces the enzyme's affinity for its substrate [ev_001]. When an allosteric inhibitor binds, the active sites on the protein subunits change slightly so that they bind their substrates with less efficiency [ev_001]. This reduces enzyme activity, because the enzyme no longer effectively catalyzes the conversion of substrate to product [ev_001]. An allosteric activator also binds to a location on the enzyme away from the active site, inducing a conformational change that increases the affinity of the active site for its substrate [ev_002]. In allosteric activation, the activator molecule modifies the shape of the active site to allow a better fit of the substrate [ev_002]. The inhibitor and activator therefore differ in their effect on the active site's shape and substrate affinity, and in the direction of their effect on enzyme activity: the inhibitor makes the active site fit the substrate less well and lowers activity, while the activator makes it fit better and raises activity [ev_001] [ev_002].","short_answer":null,"citations":["ev_001","ev_002"],"refusal_reason":null,"follow_up_questions":[],"confidence":0.8,"tutor_question":null,"learner_attempt_evaluation":null}
